title: Only what he strives for
hook: a person has only what he strives for, and his striving will be seen (53:39–40)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muntaha, the farthest limit, and your line was the farthest tree. Did a tree, or an edge, stop you for a moment? Day six hundred.

Day six hundred. However those mornings came, with full attention, half-asleep, or pressed play just to keep the streak alive, they were somebody's effort. A milestone invites a tally: days, streaks, minutes. Surah An-Najm, today's verse, keeps a different kind of tally. It's about what a person ends up holding at the end. Not what they hoped for, not what they inherited, not what someone said about them. What they actually strove for, and nothing else.

Surah An-Najm, verses thirty-nine and forty. Pickthall's translation: "And that man hath only that for which he maketh effort, And that his effort will be seen." The word is sa'y, striving, effort, going toward something on purpose. If you've followed the pilgrimage, you've met it. The sa'y is the walk, seven times, between the hills of Safa and Marwah, remembering Hajar running between them searching for water for her baby, Isma'il. Same word. Effort as a body moving toward what it needs. The verse sits in a passage the surah says was in the scrolls of Musa and of Ibrahim: that no soul carries another's burden, and that a person has only what they strive for. Two promises come out of it. First, nobody can take your effort from you, or be credited with it in your place. Second, it will be seen. Not necessarily by people. Seen. Here the scholars raise an honest question. What about charity given for the dead, or prayers for a parent who's gone? Hadith in Bukhari and Muslim say such things do reach the dead. Scholars reconcile it in different ways. Some say a righteous child is part of the parent's own striving: a hadith in Muslim names a good child who prays for you among the three things that continue after death. Others say the verse sets the rule of justice, and Allah's generosity can add to it. Either way, the verse's core stands: in its words, a person's effort is theirs, and it will be seen.
screen: `SA'Y: EFFORT TOWARD A NEED.` · `HAJAR, BETWEEN SAFA AND MARWAH.` · `YOURS, AND IT WILL BE SEEN.` · `WHAT REACHES THE DEAD? SCHOLARS WEIGH IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: strive at one thing today. Sit, and breathe. Picture Hajar's walk: back and forth between two hills, looking, not giving up. Now choose one thing today that deserves your real effort: a hard conversation, a task you keep postponing, a skill you're learning, a person who needs you. Picture yourself doing it fully, not halfway. Feel what it would be like to finish. If you pray, you can ask for strength in it. The bell holds the time.
Sa'y: in 53:39, a person has only their effort, and in 53:40, that effort will be seen. Today's word.
Your line: only what you strive for. Today, give your real effort to the one thing you chose, and let it be seen by whoever sees. Day six hundred.

howItsDone: Pilgrims perform the sa'y, walking seven times between Safa and Marwah in memory of Hajar; Muslims also give charity and pray on behalf of parents who have died, as hadith describe.
